findings.evidence: CODEOWNERS lines 32–37 confirm all six wildcard rules added in fix-round 1: docs/security/** @jrnb2024 (closes SAFE-001 + SAFE-007), output/findings/** @jrnb2024 (closes SAFE-002 + SAFE-003 + SAFE-004), docs/adoption/** @jrnb2024 (closes SAFE-005), docs/plans/** @jrnb2024 (closes SAFE-006), output/control-tower/** @jrnb2024 and output/ci/** @jrnb2024 (closes SAFE-008). Each target file confirmed present and subsumed by the matching wildcard. ORDERING INVARIANT comment (SAFE-009) present at CODEOWNERS lines 18–24 and accurately describes last-match-wins semantics.
findings.impact: All R1 MAJ + MIN blocking surfaces resolved. This finding is informational only.

findings.claim: tests/workflow/** fixture files (expected-annotations.json, services.yml) are not covered by CODEOWNERS, creating a workflow-selftest harness bypass vector that allows policy-check enforcement to be silently weakened.
findings.evidence: Glob of tests/workflow/** confirms: tests/workflow/fixture-fail/expected-annotations.json, tests/workflow/fixture-pass/expected-annotations.json, tests/workflow/fixture-fail/services.yml, tests/workflow/fixture-pass/services.yml all exist and are NOT covered by any CODEOWNERS rule. CODEOWNERS covers tests/conflict_gate/** @jrnb2024 but has no rule for tests/workflow/**. Per WP-SCP-020 §4 020B.1: 'SCP-local job workflow-selftest trigger = pull_request on paths .github/workflows/policy-check.yml, policies/**, tests/workflow/**, schemas/policy-check-summary.schema.json'. The workflow itself (.github/workflows/policy-check.yml, .github/workflows/workflow-selftest.yml) IS covered by .github/workflows/** @jrnb2024. The expected-annotations.json files define what the selftest considers a passing run — they are the ground-truth assertions for the harness.
findings.impact: A PR that modifies tests/workflow/fixture-fail/expected-annotations.json to expect empty annotations (or to match any output) would require no CODEOWNERS-mandated review. With weakened expected output, the workflow-selftest CI job passes even when policy-check.yml stops emitting error annotations for policy violations. Attack chain: (1) PR-A: modify fixture-fail/expected-annotations.json to accept empty annotations — no CODEOWNERS review triggered; selftest still passes because expectations now match empty output. (2) PR-B: modify policy-check.yml to suppress annotation emission for a class of violations — requires @jrnb2024 review, but selftest no longer catches the regression. The harness that guards policy enforcement correctness is itself unguarded. This is particularly dangerous because workflow-selftest is the only automated CI signal that policy-check.yml annotations fire correctly against known violations.
findings.mitigation: Add tests/workflow/** @jrnb2024 to CODEOWNERS. This should appear after tests/conflict_gate/** @jrnb2024 in the governance block (per ORDERING INVARIANT). Separately, consider whether the broader tests/** or tests/scripts/** surfaces warrant coverage — tests/scripts/test_empty_sha_bypass.py and test_scp_policy_check.py test bypass-detection scripts, but those test files assert deny behaviour rather than define expected outputs, so they are lower-severity than the fixture files.

(3) Last-match-wins: the new broad rule silently overrides docs/security/**, docs/adoption/**, docs/plans/**, docs/DECISIONS.md, output/findings/**, output/control-tower/**, output/ci/** — removing @jrnb2024 governance from all of them. (4) Subsequent PRs touching those paths now require review from @other instead of @jrnb2024. In solo-operator mode with require_review_from_non_author=false, the practical impact is limited (all PRs are self-approved regardless). However, when a second maintainer is added and require_review_from_non_author is flipped to true, this gap allows CODEOWNERS to be modified without the second maintainer's review — defeating the governance structure at the moment it becomes meaningful.
findings.mitigation: Add /CODEOWNERS @jrnb2024 as the final line of the governance block (last-match-wins ensures this specific rule governs the file even if a broad wildcard precedes it). In solo-operator mode this requires self-approval of CODEOWNERS changes (no change in practice). When a second maintainer joins and require_review_from_non_author is flipped, CODEOWNERS changes will also require their review — which is the desired posture. This one-line fix is the minimum viable enforcement mechanism available without a CI linting script.

findings.claim: The ORDERING INVARIANT is documentation-only with no machine enforcement; a careless PR could violate it without any automated signal.
findings.evidence: CODEOWNERS lines 18–24 contain an accurate ORDERING INVARIANT comment. No CI job validates CODEOWNERS ordering. No script at scripts/ checks that no broad wildcard rule appears after the specific governance block. The comment instructs 'Re-verify ordering whenever this file is touched' but relies entirely on human compliance. R2-SAFE-015 demonstrates that CODEOWNERS doesn't even require review for changes to itself, so the human re-verification step has no enforcement gate.
findings.impact: A careless future PR adding a broad docs/** rule for a legitimate reason (e.g., docs coverage for a new team member) after line 37 silently overrides the specific governance rules with no automated warning. The only signal is the ORDERING INVARIANT comment, which requires the author to know to read it and understand last-match-wins semantics. Compared to the risk accepted in SAFE-009 (nit, already closed), this is the residual enforcement gap after the comment was added — the comment is necessary but not sufficient.
findings.mitigation: (1) Minimum: close R2-SAFE-015 first (add /CODEOWNERS @jrnb2024). This ensures any CODEOWNERS ordering violation at least requires @jrnb2024 review. (2) Optional but recommended: add a scripts/check-codeowners-order.sh that asserts (a) no broad wildcard rule (matching docs/**, output/**, or *) appears after line N of the governance block, and (b) /CODEOWNERS is present as the last governance rule. Wire to .github/workflows/workflow-selftest.yml or a dedicated lint job. Without (2), the ordering invariant relies solely on author discipline.

findings.claim: docs/integrations/** (conflict-gate doctrine + MCP error code reference) is not covered by CODEOWNERS; governance-adjacent documentation can be tampered to mislead operators.
findings.evidence: Glob of docs/integrations/** confirms two files: docs/integrations/conflict-gate.md and docs/integrations/mcp-error-codes.md. Neither is covered by any CODEOWNERS rule (docs/DECISIONS.md, docs/security/**, docs/adoption/**, docs/plans/** are covered; docs/integrations/** is not). conflict-gate.md documents the SCP-E005 conflict-gate doctrine — the merge-block behavior and adjudication path that operators follow when Rego and Python disagree. mcp-error-codes.md documents SCP-E001..E006 error codes referenced throughout the specification.
findings.impact: Tamper conflict-gate.md to describe SCP-E005 as advisory rather than merge-blocking. Operators following the tampered doc would treat conflict-gate disagreements as non-blocking, degrading the governance posture without touching any code. This is a social-engineering bypass rather than a technical one — the CI behavior is unchanged, but human operators in the adjudication loop are misled. Severity is nit because: (1) the actual merge-block behavior is in code (CI job rego-vs-python-conflict), not in this doc; (2) the primary audience is developers already familiar with the codebase; (3) the attack requires physical access to the repo. mcp-error-codes.md is lower-sensitivity (reference documentation only).
findings.mitigation: Add docs/integrations/** @jrnb2024 to CODEOWNERS. This closes the documentation-as-social-engineering vector for the conflict-gate doctrine doc without adding disproportionate governance overhead. Alternatively, accept as known-residual given the low practical impact — flag in a CODEOWNERS.md annotation as a known uncovered path.

findings.claim: §8 bus-factor-1 rewrite assessment: NO regression detected. The 'accepted operational exposure' framing is accurate and the escalation path is complete for the personal-account closure.
findings.evidence: WP-SCP-020-policy-federation-primitive.md line 188 (post fix-round 1): '[LIVE] Bus factor on adjudication + break-glass approval (accepted operational risk). ... Accepted as operational exposure for v1.0.0; escalation path: when a second maintainer joins the estate, (a) add them to CODEOWNERS, (b) flip require_review_from_non_author to true, (c) amend this risk row to [CLOSED]. Review quarterly; re-evaluate at 2026-07-21.' The pre-fix text contained stale scp-break-glass team references that would have caused an operator to attempt adding a maintainer to a team that was never created (CG-MAJ-001). The new text is factually correct for the personal-account/single-operator closure: no team created, escalation path is 3 concrete steps, [LIVE] badge is present, review date is live in STATUS.md line 64 and auto-memory project_scheduled_followups.md.
findings.impact: No weakening. The framing 'accepted operational exposure' is standard risk-acceptance language. The escalation path specifies steps (a)(b)(c) which are more actionable than the broken pre-fix text. The only theoretical gap — no stated consequence if the 2026-07-21 review finds no second maintainer — is not a regression from the original (which was broken), and is acceptable for a v1.0.0 operational risk acceptance. SAFE-011 (nit, deferred) covers the automated enforcement gap for the review date itself.
findings.mitigation: No action required on §8 framing. The bus-factor-1 risk row is accurately documented and appropriately scoped. If stronger enforcement is desired, close SAFE-011 by automating the 2026-07-21 review trigger.
